articles.title: Delhi-NCR knew, so why didn't it act?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi-NCR has been witnessing a spate of incidents in the past few days that do not seem to have much in common on the face of it — a traff.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi-NCR has been witnessing a spate of incidents in the past few days that do not seem to have much in common on the face of it — a traffic signal pole crashing on vehicles at Delhi's Minto Road, action on unauthorized construction and illegal PGs in Gurgaon, road rage and hit-and-run cases and disruptions to public transport. But look closer, and you start to see a familiar pattern. Sometimes there were warning signs, violations or risks well before the incident itself. The bigger question is whether the region's civic and enforcement systems are doing enough to act on those warning signs before they turn into accidents or public crises.When accident is preceded by warningSuch a case is the collapse of a traffic signal pole on vehicles at Minto Road in central Delhi on Tuesday night. Two people were hurt when the pole came down, and police are investigating whether seepage and rust weakened its base. The pole was installed in 2010 and was reportedly showing some visible wear, such as rust around the bottom. More importantly, sources said the agency that maintains it had been alerted to the need for repairs about five days before the collapse. That makes the incident more than a matter of why the pole fell. It poses the more uncomfortable question of what happened in between the warning and the accident.Infrastructure in a city usually does not suddenly break down without some indication that it is deteriorating. Rusts, cracks, water seepages, loose fixtures, damaged pavements and broken street lights can remain visible for weeks or months. The problem is not often identifying the problem, but getting someone to own it, record it, fix it and check that the repair has actually been done. If that chain breaks at any point, what might have been a fairly routine maintenance issue can quickly become a public safety incident.From illegal PGs to illegal floorsThe latest drive of enforcement in Gurgaon is yet another take on the same problem. The Department of Town and Country Planning on Wednesday resumed action in Sushant Lok-1 and South City-1 against unauthorized additional floors, commercial activity in residential buildings, illegal PGs and misuse of stilt parking. More than 17 properties were sealed or faced demolition in the latest operation, after about 27 properties were targeted in two earlier campaigns. In one case, a property with 23 rooms allegedly being used as an illegal PG was sealed by authorities.The numbers also show why sealing properties one at a time may not be enough. For years, Gurgaon has been grappling with conversion of residential properties into commercial establishments, unauthorized construction and the growing use of houses as paying-guest accommodation. Once additional floors are constructed, rooms are carved out and a residential property starts behaving like a commercial property, making it far more difficult to reverse the process. Enforcement may be necessary, but the greater challenge is preventing a violation from becoming a fixture in a neighborhood in the first place.It is not simply about individual houses. The recent cases of illegal colonies around the 900-metre restricted zone near the IAF ammunition depot has once again thrown the spotlight on construction in the area, although there are long-standing restrictions. The question for a city like Gurgaon, which is growing so fast, is not just how many buildings can be sealed in an enforcement drive. And it’s also how fast authorities can detect unauthorized activity and prevent it from turning into a whole cluster of infringements.Road safety an event driven businessThe road-rage incident on Gurgaon’s Golf Course Road brings the issue to a more personal setting. Footage shot on her motorbike, as well as CCTV footage, proved to be vital to the investigation into a woman on a motorbike being chased and rammed by a car. The police have constituted a five-member SIT and arrested two accused and taken them into custody for crime-scene reconstruction. The FIR was later enhanced to include charges relating to stalking, outraging the modesty of a woman and attempt to murder.Another incident in Greater Noida demonstrated how quickly a routine road journey can become life-changing injuries. A 32-year-old man met with an accident in wee hours of September 5 when he was hit by a car at Ek Murti Chowk. He suffered multiple fractures in his legs, hand, knees and spine. The 24-year-old driver was later arrested and the vehicle impounded by police. The facts are different from the Gurgaon road-rage incident, but both highlight the same vulnerability: speed, aggression or poor road discipline entering equation can turn a normal journey into a serious safety incident in seconds.There is also an increasing reliance on cameras and video to reconstruct what happened after an incident. Increasingly, police are using CCTV footage, dashcams and recordings on mobile phones to identify vehicles, establish sequences of events and find suspects. That helps with investigation, but it's ultimately a response mechanism. The tougher job is to build the roads and enforcement regimes that catch and deter reckless behavior before anyone gets hurt.The city’s safety net is strainedThe issue is not only about physical infrastructure or road behavior. Haryana’s H1N1 count rose from 163 on August 26 to 378 on September 16, while in Gurgaon it soared from 12 to 46. Admissions to hospitals across the state more than doubled from 27 to 58 during the same period. These numbers place a different kind of strain on the city’s safety net. It’s not as visible as a fallen pole or a shuttered building, but it can quickly affect hospitals, families and workplaces.Public transit is vulnerable in its own ways. Commuters in several areas in Delhi were left with fewer options and increased demand for the Metro and app-based transport after a strike by contractual DTC drivers over wages and social-security benefits hit bus services. Commuters feel the effect immediately. If there is a problem in one part of the transport network, it can quickly lead to overcrowding and congestion elsewhere, especially during rush hour.These incidents are of very different types, taken one by one. A rusty signal pole is an engineering and maintenance problem. An illegal PG is an enforcement problem. Road rage is a law-and-order and road-safety problem. Rising infections put a strain on public health. A bus strike affects the reliability of public transport. But together they pose a larger question about how Delhi-NCR manages risk.The best safety system is the one that doesn’t have to wait for something to happen to make it work. A damaged structure requires a warning to lead to a repair. Before another floor is added, an unauthorized floor needs to be detected. You need to punish dangerous driving before a crash, not after a crash. Public services need to be robust enough to withstand disruptions and not strand commuters. For a zone developing as fast as Delhi-NCR, the true test of urban safety might therefore be less about how fast authorities respond after something goes wrong and more about how often they manage to prevent it from going wrong in the first place.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Govt debunks Pakistan claim that IAF MiG-29 crashed during landing due to pilot error
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The press information bureau (PIB) fact check unit on Thursday debunked a social media claim that an Indian Air Force (IAF) MiG-29 fighter .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The press information bureau (PIB) fact check unit on Thursday debunked a social media claim that an Indian Air Force (IAF) MiG-29 fighter jet had crashed during landing due to pilot error. They stated that the video being circulated was footage from a video game.The fact-checking unit warned that the video was being circulated by Pakistani propaganda accounts and called the claim fake.“Pakistani propaganda accounts are circulating a video with the claim that an IAF MiG-29 fighter jet crashed during landing due to pilot error,” PIB Fact Check said in a post on X, adding, “Beware! This claim is #Fake.”The unit said the footage was from War Thunder, a military combat video game featuring aircraft, land and naval vehicles.The video circulating on social media shows a fighter jet crashing while attempting to land, followed by the pilot ejecting and parachuting to safety. The footage was presented online as an actual IAF MiG-29 crash by certain accounts based out of Pakistan.PIB Fact Check urged users to report suspicious content related to the Government of India through its official channels.The claim is part of a recurring pattern of propagandist accounts circulating unrelated military accidents and video-game footage are circulated as evidence of recent events.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Call for £375k elected mayor referendum rejected in Bedford
articles.summary: Politicians vote against a motion to have a residents' poll on abolishing the post of mayor.
articles.body:
An attempt to force a referendum on whether an elected mayor should be abolished has failed.

Councillors in Bedford rejected a Labour motion to let residents decide the future of the role.

They were told a referendum would cost £375,000 to organise.

Opponents of the elected mayor system said the poll could still happen if enough residents signed a petition.

Bedford has had an elected mayor since 2002, when residents voted in favour of the move in a referendum.

The leader of the Labour group, Abu Sultan, told a meeting of the full council on Wednesday that, after more than 20 years, it was time to give the people a chance to vote again.

Sultan added that the motion was "not about settling a political score with any particular person".

Carl Meader (Labour, Kempston South) said abolishing the role would save money and the referendum would give people under 40 their first chance to vote on the issue.

Others said it was difficult to remove a serving mayor and noted the current incumbent had remained in post, despite a vote of no confidence in his leadership .

Opponents questioned whether spending £375,000 on a referendum was a valid use of the council's money.

The current mayor, Tom Wootton (Conservative, Wyboston), told the meeting he had not seen "Bedford residents marching through the streets demanding a referendum".

Christine McHugh (Liberal Democrat, Goldington) said she had originally campaigned against having an elected mayor but "found, to my surprise, that the public seemed to like the system as there was a clearly identifiable, responsible individual, and the buck stopped there".

Labour has 12 seats on the council, while the Conservatives have 14 and the Liberal Democrats have 13.

When it came to the vote, 16 councillors voted for a referendum while 24 opposed it.

The Liberal Democrat leader, Henry Vann, said: "The vote in the end wasn't even close at 24 to 16.

"So, frankly, we now need to all, as councillors of all parties, actually get down to the job of protecting services and sorting out the financial crisis at Borough Hall."

Zara Layne (Labour, Harpur) said: "I think it was a shame that residents aren't going to get a chance to have their voice heard on a matter that we believe as a Labour group is really important."

If a referendum had been successful and the post of mayor had been abolished, it is likely that the council would have adopted a strong leader model.

The full council would have elected a leader who would then select a cabinet.

One advantage of that system would be the ability of the full council to remove a leader, something that councils cannot do with an elected mayor.

But opponents argue that a strong leader system puts too much power in the hands of one person who residents had no say in appointing.

articles.title: North Carolina acquired more than 342 acres without using local purchase money; the mountain property is now moving toward becoming Buncombe County's largest public park
articles.summary: US News: A 342-acre mountain property west of Asheville has moved another step closer to becoming a public park, with Buncombe County now developing the master.
articles.body: A 342-acre mountain property west of Asheville has moved another step closer to becoming a public park, with Buncombe County now developing the master plan for what it says will be the largest park in its portfolio. The county completed the acquisition of Deaverview Mountain in March 2026 using 100% grant funding, and on September 15 approved a $1.39 million contract to begin planning the future park. According to Buncombe County, the property includes a 3,118-foot peak, 180-degree views of the French Broad River Valley, 16 headwater streams and extensive forest habitat.342 acres acquired without local purchase moneyThe Deaverview Mountain acquisition represents a major conservation project for Buncombe County, but the county did not use local purchase money to acquire the land. According to its latest update, the 342-plus-acre property was acquired using 100% grant funding, through the Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy (SAHC) and grants from the North Carolina Land and Water Fund and the federal Outdoor Recreation Legacy Partnership (ORLP) programme. The county's project page lists an ORLP acquisition grant of $4,009,648 and a $4,162,000 North Carolina Land and Water Fund grant for acquisition and transaction costs. The county has separately set aside $7.7 million from its Open Space Bond for costs associated with the broader Deaverview project, while it plans to pursue additional grants for future development and operations.The distinction is important because acquiring the property and developing it into a functioning public park are separate stages. The land has been secured, but trails, access facilities and other visitor infrastructure still need to be planned and built.Mountain landscape with views and waterwaysDeaverview Mountain sits west of Asheville and contains a 3,118-foot summit overlooking the French Broad River Valley. The property has open areas with 180-degree views, expansive forested habitat and 16 headwater streams, including one identified as a priority for state protection. A conservation easement covers 315 acres of the property, according to the county. The county envisions the site primarily for passive recreation and nature-based activities. Potential uses include hiking, nature viewing and outdoor education, while the planning process will also consider how to protect biodiversity, water quality and the mountain's natural landscape.The location gives the project an additional conservation dimension. Deaverview Mountain is a prominent landscape around Asheville, and Buncombe County has described the acquisition as an opportunity to protect a significant natural asset from future development while creating new public access to trails and scenic overlooks.From private property to future public parkThe path to public ownership began before the county completed its purchase. In 2023, a conservation-minded buyer acquired the Deaverview Mountain property and entered into a three-year option agreement with the Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy. That arrangement provided time to identify a permanent conservation solution. SAHC and Buncombe County subsequently worked together to secure the funding needed to protect the property and eventually transfer it into county ownership.The county closed on the property on March 19, 2026. At that point, however, Deaverview Mountain did not immediately become a public recreation area. The county states that the property remains closed to the public and will not open until the necessary park infrastructure has been completed. That means the current phase is focused on turning the newly acquired landscape into a carefully planned park rather than opening the mountain immediately to visitors.$1.39 million master-plan contract approvedThe next major step came at the Buncombe County Board of Commissioners' September 15 meeting. Commissioners approved a $1.39 million contract with Equinox Environmental to develop the Deaverview Mountain Master Plan and engineering designs. The two-phase planning contract will cover community outreach, environmental and trail assessments, recommendations for future funding, and plans for access, parking, trails, restrooms and viewsheds. A future third phase is anticipated to focus on actually constructing trails, access improvements and viewshed amenities.The county had already issued a request for qualifications for design services in March, shortly after acquiring the property. Its project documents describe the future Deaverview Mountain Park as a way to expand the county's park system while preserving an important natural landscape.What the future park could offerAlthough the exact layout of the park has not yet been determined, the planning documents provide an indication of what visitors could eventually experience. The county has identified hiking, nature viewing, outdoor education and other passive recreation as potential uses. The mountain's summit and open areas could provide scenic viewpoints, while its forests and waterways offer opportunities for environmental education and habitat conservation.The project also has a conservation component that will shape future development. The county says its goals include protecting water quality, preserving biodiversity and safeguarding natural habitats. The conservation easement covering much of the property adds another layer of protection as the park is planned.Toward Buncombe County's largest parkOnce completed, Deaverview Mountain is expected to become the largest park in Buncombe County's current portfolio. County officials described the acquisition as a major step toward creating the largest park in the county's portfolio, although the proposed 1,600-acre Pisgah View State Park would be larger if it proceeds as planned.For now, Deaverview Mountain remains a protected property in transition. The land has been acquired, the conservation framework is in place and the master-planning process is underway. What remains is to determine exactly how trails, access points, parking, restrooms and scenic areas can be introduced without undermining the mountain landscape that the acquisition was intended to protect. The result will be a public park built around a landscape that, until recently, was not publicly accessible. With the acquisition funded entirely through grants and the planning phase now moving forward, the 342-acre mountain is gradually shifting from protected private land into a future destination for hiking, conservation and outdoor education.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: "Every race teaches me that age is...": Meet 69-year-old Kishori Kudecha, who started running marathons at 60, found confidence and a whole new life
articles.summary: Kishori Kudecha did not grow up as an athlete, and she did not start running in her twenties or thirties either. At the age of 60, this homemaker, mot.
articles.body: Kishori Kudecha did not grow up as an athlete, and she did not start running in her twenties or thirties either. At the age of 60, this homemaker, mother of two, and grandmother of three decided to take up running, a decision that has since turned into a full-blown second life built around fitness and endurance. Kishori is part of the WalkAbout athlete programme, a community-driven platform built for adults aged 55 and above that aims to change how ageing is perceived in urban India. She is, in fact, WalkAbout's first sponsored athlete. In an Instagram video, she shared that her very first run was a 5 km race, and remarkably, she earned a podium finish in it too.From a 2 km jog to 45 podium finishesSince that first run, Kishori's progress has been steady and, by most standards, extraordinary. She has gone on to complete 8 km, 10 km, 16 km, 21 km, and 35 km ultra marathon distances before finally completing her first full 42 km marathon at the Tata Mumbai Marathon in 2024. In December 2025, she pushed even further, completing a 50 km ultramarathon with Pinkathon Invincible Women. Along this journey, Kishori has secured more than 45 podium finishes, consistently placing among the top three runners in the 45 plus to 65 plus age categories. Her racing journey has taken her across several Indian cities, including Ahmedabad, Goa, Surat, Pune, Ratnagiri, Satara, Mount Abu, and Valsad. Her achievements have not gone unnoticed. She received the Best 1st Runner Up Award in the Super Veteran category from Mumbai Road Runners in 2025, followed by a 2nd Runner Up Award in March 2026. On March 8, 2026, she was also honoured with the Best Runner Award by Swami Vivekanand Youth.In her own wordsKishori has spoken openly about what led her to running and what it has meant for her life since. Describing her starting point, she said she began running at 60 with the Sketchers group, largely as a way to stay fit and healthy and to prove that "age is just a number" and there is no barrier to chasing one's dreams. What started as a 2 km run eventually grew into 5Ks, 10Ks, half marathons, and ultimately 35 km and 50 km ultra runs. She has credited running with genuinely transforming her life, saying it has made her considerably more confident. Speaking about what keeps her going, she has also said in a separate interaction shared by WalkAbout that every race teaches her that age is just a number and that today she feels stronger, happier, and more energetic than ever before. Her hope, as she has put it, is simple: that her journey encourages others to start too, no matter their age.Fitness as a way of life, not a phaseWhat makes Kishori's story resonate is not just the number of medals or the distances covered, but the mindset behind it. For her, fitness is not a temporary goal or a passing phase; it is, in her own description, a way of life. At 69, she continues to train and compete alongside runners decades younger, steadily challenging the assumption that physical ambition has an age limit. Her story adds to a growing, quietly powerful conversation around active ageing in India, one that pushes back against the idea that a woman past 60 should slow down, step back, or stop setting new physical goals. Kishori's own journey suggests otherwise, showing that with the right support and mindset, the most demanding chapters of a fitness journey can begin well after most people assume it is too late to start.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: In 2023, a meteorite blasted from Mars was found by a hunter in Earth’s Sahara Desert; the 54-pound rock was later sold at Sotheby’s in 2025 for $5.3 million
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In a landmark auction at Sotheby's, a 54-pound meteorite from Mars, known as NWA 16788, was sold for a staggering $5.3 million, raising questions about international meteorite trade and ownership.
articles.body: The majority of rocks found in the middle of a desert remain just that: ordinary stones that have been sculpted over thousands of years by heat and wind. Occasionally, however, someone discovers a rock that has no right to be there, having come from somewhere other than the immediate surroundings. On 16 July 2023, a meteorite hunter found a single 24.67-kilogram stone in the Kefkaf region of Niger’s Agadez area; it was later classified as a Martian shergottite.The rock, eventually designated as Northwest Africa 16788, or NWA 16788 for short, weighed a hefty 54 pounds, around the weight of a car tyre, and was over 15 inches across at its widest point. Meteorite hunting is itself a specialised activity, and deserts like the Sahara are desirable hunting grounds precisely because their bare, rock-free stretches of sand make an out-of-place stone far simpler to find than it would be in practically any other place on Earth.Confirming a piece of another planetFinding a strange-looking rock is one thing, demonstrating where it truly came from is a whole other issue. The reddish colour and glassy fusion crust on NWA 16788 were early indicators that something remarkable had been found, but further laboratory investigation of the rock’s mineral and gas makeup was needed to prove the scientific significance of the find. NWA 16788 was classified as an olivine microgabbroic shergottite, an igneous type of Martian meteorite whose mineral texture records its crystallization history, in the Meteoritical Bulletin Database, the official database of approved meteorite names and classifications. Its Martian origin was confirmed by matching the gases contained in the rock to the atmospheric measurements by NASA’s Viking landers in the 1970s. The Meteoritical Bulletin entry also records that the stone was found on 16 July 2023 in the Kefkaf region of Niger, with a 24.67-kilogram main mass and a single piece recovered. Its description identifies a porphyritic rock with olivine phenocrysts up to 3 millimetres across, shock-melted areas and chemically zoned olivine and pyroxene ranging from pigeonite to augite.That placed NWA 16788 in the company of a very few indeed. Of all meteorites ever found on Earth, just a small fraction came from Mars. NASA estimates that more than 50,000 meteorites have been recovered on Earth, and the Martian material is a small fraction of that total, roughly equal to the number of meteorites known to have originated from the Moon. NWA 16788 was unusually large even among Martian meteorites. Sotheby’s said the specimen represented nearly 7% of the total known mass of Martian material on Earth and was about 70% larger than the next-largest known piece. The 24.67-kilogram stone is also the largest individual Martian meteorite recorded in the Meteoritical Bulletin Database.From a private gallery in Tuscany to a saleroom in New YorkBefore ever going to auction, the meteorite was displayed to the public at the Italian Space Agency in Rome for European Researchers’ Night in 2024, before spending some time in a private exhibition in Tuscany. In July 2025, it was a real moment of recognition when Sotheby’s put it at the centre of a natural history sale in New York, officially branding it as the largest piece of Mars ever found on Earth. Sotheby noted that the meteorite showed very little terrestrial weathering, suggesting that it had spent relatively little time exposed to Earth’s surface environment.Before the sale, Sotheby's had predicted the meteorite would bring somewhere between two and four million dollars. The auction began with two advance bids already in place, and the tension grew as phone and online bidders competed until the gavel fell, far exceeding expectations. Including the hammer at 4.3 million dollars, the total amount, including fees and taxes, was just above 5.3 million dollars, making NWA 16788 immediately the most expensive meteorite ever sold at auction.A record sale that posed unpleasant questionsSotheby’s executives said they have never disclosed the buyer’s identity, which is not uncommon for high-value natural history sales of this nature. What happened next was anything but normal. After the sale, questions were raised in Niger about how the meteorite had been removed from the country, prompting authorities to investigate its discovery and export.The dispute revealed a true grey area in the entire realm of the meteorite trade, where the international rules about ownership and export of space rocks that are found on private or public land differ wildly from country to country, and enforcement in far-flung desert regions is often difficult at best. Whatever the result of the inquiry into Niger, NWA 16788 has already earned its status as a scientific milestone. The rock was blasted from Mars by an ancient impact, travelled roughly 140 million miles through space and eventually reached Earth before being found in Niger and sold for millions of dollars; a reminder that fragments of planetary history can sometimes turn up in the most unexpected places.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2017, Hurricane Irma emptied Barbuda and left pets behind; when people returned, abandoned dogs had begun acting feral and were hunting livestock
articles.summary: US News: The aftermath of Hurricane Irma in Barbuda revealed a shocking crisis as abandoned pets turned feral, hunting for livestock. This article explores the impact of the disaster on animals left behind and the steps taken for recovery.
articles.body: Above all, evacuation instructions are based on one thing: that people come first and everything else may wait. That rationale is sound when a Category 5 hurricane is about to hit a small island. But the evacuation created an immediate problem that disaster plans often struggle to address: what happens to animals left behind? Hundreds of pets and thousands of farm animals were left with nowhere to go and no one to feed them. And exactly that happened on the Caribbean island of Barbuda in September 2017 when Hurricane Irma forced Barbuda’s residents to evacuate the island, leaving pets and livestock behind.At its peak, Irma hit Barbuda, the smaller of the two islands that make up Antigua and Barbuda. The storm destroyed or damaged almost 95 per cent of the island’s structures, leaving it without water or communications and making Barbuda practically uninhabitable, the National Hurricane Centre said. Irma destroyed about 95% of Barbuda’s infrastructure and forced its roughly 1,800 residents to evacuate to Antigua; after Hurricane Jose approached days later, the remaining residents also left, leaving the island temporarily without its population.Animals left to fend for themselvesThe evacuation could not take the animals with it. Dogs, cats, cows, horses and other animals were left to roam freely over a landscape no longer divided by fences, pens and shelter, because most of the structures that had once held them were crushed by Irma’s storms. In the immediate aftermath of the storm, Karen Corbin, president of the Antigua and Barbuda Humane Society, was one of the first responders to arrive on the island, and what she found frightened her enough to issue a public warning almost immediately.Corbin was more concerned about the pets. Hundreds of former pets, abandoned by their owners and growing hungrier, started to exhibit early indications of going wild within days, and she warned that without intervention they would eventually start hunting the animals now roaming unsecured throughout Barbuda’s farms. Local farmers, many of whom had left cattle behind thinking they would be returning in a week or two, watched the crisis unfold from Antigua with no way to get back and intervene.The prediction comes trueIt wasn’t long before that prophecy came true. Weeks became months as Barbuda struggled to recover, far more slowly than anybody had planned. Packs of canines, some of them family pets just weeks before, began preying on the very goats, sheep and poultry that had survived the hurricane itself. Farmers who returned to rebuild found that dogs, which had recently been household pets, had attacked some of their surviving livestock. Cats were also affected, hiding from wandering groups of dogs and finding it particularly difficult to source food in the aftermath. World Animal Protection reported that its response teams found distressed animals and warned that hungry dogs and pigs could attack livestock. Animal welfare groups hurried to respond, setting up temporary shelters in whatever facilities were available, including one damaged hotel that residents started calling the Dog Hotel, where rescued animals were placed until a true long-term refuge was created. Volunteers drove around the island, feeding and treating whatever animals they could reach, while others worked to reunite pets with owners who had been forced to leave without them, sometimes making the difficult decision to euthanise dogs that were too far along in their transformation to be safely rehomed.Recovery, slowly and unevenlyBarbuda’s human recovery was slow, with many islanders opting to stay on Antigua permanently rather than rebuild homes that Irma had reduced to ruins. Shiraz Hopkins, a farmer who returned, often found himself patching fences and replacing sheep lost to attacks by feral dogs, while urging local officials to speed up the restoration of electricity, water and schools. The animal crisis eased gradually as more loose dogs found their way to shelters and farmers put the fencing that had separated predator from prey back together, but the episode lingered as a reminder of how quickly domesticated animals could begin behaving differently when the structures and human care around them disappeared.What happened in Barbuda has become a kind of case study for disaster preparedness agencies around the Caribbean, exposing a hole that evacuation protocols don’t often cover: what to do with an island’s animals when its inhabitants can’t take them with them. The dogs were responding to a landscape in which food, shelter and human control had suddenly disappeared, while the livestock were left exposed to predators in an environment very different from the one they had known before the storm.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Connecticut homeowner built a bridge to protect his property from erosion; judge ordered him to restore the brook as town says work needed a permit
articles.summary: US News: A 74-year-old homeowner in Bethel, Connecticut, has been ordered to address unpermitted work along a brook behind his property after a dispute with th.
articles.body: A 74-year-old homeowner in Bethel, Connecticut, has been ordered to address unpermitted work along a brook behind his property after a dispute with the town reached court. Mark Bjorken built a wooded bridge across Limekiln Brook and moved rocks along its banks, saying the work was intended to protect his property from erosion and restore the area. However, Bethel’s wetlands commission determined that the work required approval. Following a neighbour’s complaint in 2023, the town directed Bjorken to restore the brook or seek a permit. On September 10, 2026, Connecticut Superior Court Judge Barbara Brazzel-Massaro upheld the commission’s decision and dismissed Bjorken’s appeal, according to the News-Times.How a bridge built to prevent erosion led to a court battleThe dispute began in 2023 after a neighbour reported that Bjorken had moved rocks and reinforced both sides of Limekiln Brook. According to the town, the work altered the flow of the brook and involved changes within a regulated wetlands area.A wetlands enforcement officer inspected the property and found moved rocks and a wooded bridge crossing the brook. Town officials subsequently directed Bjorken to restore the waterway or apply for the necessary approval from the wetlands commission.Bjorken maintained that his actions were intended to protect his property from erosion. He was concerned that the brook was moving closer to his home’s foundation, and he argued that the work was necessary maintenance and restoration rather than activity requiring a wetlands permit.Homeowner argued that the work was necessary maintenanceIn 2024, Bjorken submitted an application to the town. He argued that his activities qualified as residential landscaping, property maintenance and repairs, including the restoration and rehabilitation of his rear garden along the western bank of Limekiln Brook.The work reportedly involved removing debris from the brook and clearing diseased or dead trees that were lying in the water or likely to fall into it. Bjorken also repaired stones lining the bank, describing them as part of an existing wall that had fallen into disrepair.His argument was that these activities were intended to restore the property and address erosion, rather than introduce unauthorised changes to the waterway.Why the wetlands commission rejected his applicationBethel’s wetlands commission rejected Bjorken’s request for an exception. The commission determined that the work went beyond routine maintenance and therefore required a permit.Bjorken had argued that the work fell within an exemption for residential landscaping and property maintenance. However, the commission said he had not provided enough information or documentation to establish that the work qualified for the exemption.The central issue was whether Bjorken’s activities could legally be treated as maintenance or whether the changes to the brook and its banks required formal approval under the town’s wetlands regulations.Judge upheld the town’s decisionConnecticut Superior Court Judge Barbara Brazzel-Massaro issued a 10-page ruling on September 10, 2026. She upheld the wetlands commission’s decision and dismissed Bjorken’s appeal.The judge found that Bjorken had the responsibility to demonstrate that his work qualified for an exemption. The burden of proving the exemption applied rested with him, rather than with the commission.The ruling concluded that the commission had properly determined that work in the wetlands could not be authorised without a valid permit. The court therefore sustained the commission’s decision.Homeowner described himself as a land artistBjorken, who owns a tree service business, has described himself as a “land artist”. He said the property was an “artist’s canvas” and explained that restoration work had been part of his professional life.He purchased the home approximately 10 years ago. In defending his actions, Bjorken said he was attempting to protect his investment from erosion and prevent the brook from getting dangerously close to his home.He also reportedly said that he could stand in his bedroom, open the window and fish, highlighting how close the waterway had come to the property. Bjorken maintained that he was trying to resolve the erosion issue and indicated that he intended to continue challenging the decision.What the court ruling means for BjorkenThe ruling requires Bjorken to comply with the town’s requirements concerning the work along Limekiln Brook. He must either restore the brook to its condition before the work or apply to the wetlands commission for the appropriate permit.He also has the option of appealing the court’s decision. The ruling does not prevent him from seeking approval for work that may be permitted under the town’s regulations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1995, Anguilla fishermen watched green iguanas float toward shore on uprooted trees after Hurricane Luis helped carry them about 200 miles
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In October 1995, fishermen on Anguilla witnessed green iguanas arriving on uprooted trees after hurricanes, providing rare evidence of animal dispersal across oceans. This event challenged previous biological theories and demonstrated nature's resilience.
articles.body: For much of the twentieth century, biologists debated whether land animals could cross open oceans on floating natural debris and establish themselves on islands they could not otherwise reach. In October 1995, a fisherman on the small Caribbean island of Anguilla saw something floating towards its shores that no one had expected to see.Hurricane Luis had swept across the northern Leeward Islands as a devastating Category 4 storm weeks earlier in September 1995. Luis had produced gusts of more than 100 knots as it passed close to islands, including Guadeloupe, uprooting trees and plants over a large area of the region before passing on, a preliminary report from NOAA's Hurricane Research Division said. A second hurricane, Marilyn, arrived about a week later and added to the devastation. Neither storm was exceptional for the Caribbean’s hurricane season, but the debris they left behind in the ocean included an unexpected guest.An unexpected invasionOn 4 October 1995, fishermen off Anguilla's eastern beaches saw a giant mat of logs and uprooted trees floating towards the island, some of the trunks said to be over thirty feet long. As the battered raft came ashore over the next few days, residents discovered it was carrying living green iguanas, a species previously unknown to Anguilla. Local fisherman Cleve Webster subsequently recalled watching in disbelief as one of the animals came ashore, its tail dragging behind the wood it held onto in the sea.They had made the trek with 15 or more iguanas arriving alive but weak and dehydrated. Photographs of the reptiles were sent to Ellen Censky, a herpetologist then working at Carnegie Museum of Natural History who had studied Anguilla’s lizard fauna. She identified the animal as iguana iguana.Attempting to locate their originMore than a look was needed to confirm that the iguanas had actually rafted over open water rather than arrived in some other way. The team tracked the path of storms Luis and Marilyn, compared it with known ocean current patterns and identified the kinds of trees on the raft with vegetation known to thrive on Guadeloupe. All the evidence pointed to the same conclusion: the iguanas had been washed out to sea after storms had destroyed the trees they were resting in, then survived a journey of some 200 miles clinging to the wreckage until it eventually reached Anguilla’s coastline.The findings were reported in the 8 October 1998 issue of Nature and attracted attention because they provided unusually direct evidence for long-distance oceanic dispersal by terrestrial animals. Nature’s coverage described the finding as strong direct evidence that vertebrates could cross open water on natural rafts and establish populations on islands they could not otherwise reach. Vertebrates could disperse across oceans by rafting on natural debris and successfully colonise new islands as a result. The observation provided a concrete mechanism for a form of long-distance dispersal that fossil and genetic evidence had often suggested.A founding populationThe rafting iguanas didn’t die off quickly when they arrived, however, and instead formed a substantial breeding population on Anguilla. Censky and her team caught and tagged seven of the original arrivals for tracking purposes. When researchers returned about three years later, they found that the founding iguanas had survived and that younger animals had already hatched on the island, along with younger iguanas that had been hatched there since. What started as an accident of two hurricanes hitting within days of each other became a small, permanent addition to the wildlife of Anguilla and a rare, fully documented example of just how many of the world's island species may have arrived at their homes in the first place, not by deliberate migration but by sheer chance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Unfriendly action’: Russia blasts US sanctions bill, warns of fallout for Ukraine war
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The Kremlin on Thursday described the US House of Representatives’ passage of a sweeping Russia sanctions bill as an “unfriendly” action, warning that.
articles.body: The Kremlin on Thursday described the US House of Representatives’ passage of a sweeping Russia sanctions bill as an “unfriendly” action, warning that further US sanctions could complicate efforts to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.The comments came a day after the House passed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by 262-159. India, meanwhile, said it would take “all necessary measures” to safeguard its economic interests and ensure energy security.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia was monitoring the progress of the legislation, "We are, of course, monitoring the progress of this document. It falls under the category of unfriendly actions, and of course the imposition of any additional sanctions by the U.S. would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine."The measure now heads to US president Donald Trump and would give the administration powers to impose sanctions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas. The bill also targets Russian officials, banks, energy projects and a “shadow fleet” of tankers used to move Russian energy.The legislation was named after the late senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, who spent more than a year negotiating it. The Senate had passed the measure by 86-11 last month.The bill’s tariff provisions have particular implications for India and China, which are among the largest buyers of Russian crude. According to congressional aides cited in the supplied report, the top five purchasers of Russian crude are China, India, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan.US-mediated efforts to end the four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine have been stalled for months, but Trump sent two envoys to Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month in an effort to get the process moving again.The ministry of external affairs said New Delhi was closely monitoring developments.“As stated on several earlier occasions, India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people,” the MEA said.“It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics,” it added, saying the issue had been “discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors”.The legislation has drawn both bipartisan support and Democratic criticism in the US House. Supporters said the tariff provisions were intended to deter countries from purchasing Russian energy, while critics warned that the measure could also affect US allies and push up prices for American consumers.“For too long, Putin has bankrolled this devastating war with money and resources from countries willing to look the other way, and today, that ends,” House Speaker Mike Johnson said.Democratic opposition included concerns over the powers the legislation would give Trump. Rep. Don Beyer said supporters could regret the measure if Trump used the new authority against US allies.Meanwhile, Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal, who helped write the bill, said he hoped the sanctions would pressure Russian president Vladimir Putin towards negotiations.“To Vladimir Putin — we have your number,” Blumenthal said. “And to Ukraine — you are not alone.”Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy had urged lawmakers to approve the legislation, saying during wartime it can be better to “make a not-so-perfect decision than to do nothing”.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘No basis in international law’: China rejects US tariff threat over Russian oil
articles.summary: China News: China on Thursday rejected US efforts to pressure countries buying Russian oil and gas, saying its normal trade with other countries should not be sub.
articles.body: China on Thursday rejected US efforts to pressure countries buying Russian oil and gas, saying its normal trade with other countries should not be subject to interference or coercion by third parties.The response came after the US House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The legislation gives US President Donald Trump the power to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas, including major buyers such as China and India.Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing opposes sanctions that do not have a basis in international law or authorisation from the UN Security Council."China consistently opposes long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law and is not authorised by the United Nations Security Council," Guo said at a media briefing.He said China's trade with other countries was based on equality and mutual benefit.“Such cooperation neither targets any third party nor is subject to interference or coercion from any third party”, he said.What does the US bill propose?The US House passed the legislation by a 262-159 vote on Wednesday, after the Senate approved it last month. The bill will now go to Trump for his signature.The legislation is aimed at increasing pressure on Russia over its continuing war in Ukraine. It creates a route for the US president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas.Countries could avoid the tariff provision if they import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those purchases.India and China are among the biggest buyers of Russian crude. The proposed tariffs are therefore significant for both countries and could affect their trade with the US.China defends Russian energy tradeBeijing has repeatedly opposed unilateral sanctions and has continued economic ties with countries targeted by US sanctions, including Iran.China is also a major buyer of Russian energy. Much of its Russian oil and gas imports are transported through pipelines across the two countries' land border.Official data cited in the briefing showed China's imports of Russian oil and gas were worth about $64 billion last year. Imports between January and August this year had already crossed $70 billion.The US tariff measure could therefore put pressure on a major part of China's energy trade with Russia.India says energy security remains priorityIndia also reacted to the passage of the US bill on Thursday, saying it was monitoring developments and would take steps to protect its trade and economic interests."The government of India has noted the passage of the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in the US Congress. We are monitoring further developments on this matter. As stated on several earlier occasions, India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people. It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics," the Ministry of External Affairs said.The ministry said the potential impact of the legislation had been discussed with US officials in recent months."This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side," it added.The MEA said New Delhi would take "all necessary measures" to protect its trade and economic interests."Government will work closely with Indian trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications of these developments," it said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US committed war crimes in 2 deadly strikes in Iran; Tehran committed crimes against humanity: UN
articles.summary: Middle East News: An independent UN fact-finding mission on Iran announced on Thursday that it found US involvement in two military strikes involving a school and a spo.
articles.body: An independent UN fact-finding mission on Iran announced on Thursday that it found US involvement in two military strikes involving a school and a sports facility in February, calling them war crimes.The mission also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in their lethal crackdown on anti-government protests in late December.The report from the independent international fact-finding mission on Iran examines both America's actions during the Iran war and Tehran's handling of the nationwide unrest.According to Reuters, the report is to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council.Strike on the Minab schoolThe UN investigators said there were reasonable grounds to conclude that US forces carried out the attack on Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab. According to Iranian officials, the strikes killed more than 150, including nearly 120 schoolchildren.The mission noted that the strike caused civilian deaths and damaged civilian infrastructure, making it a war crime under international law.The report states that the US acted on intelligence indicating a senior Iranian military commander was at the location, but did not sufficiently confirm this before carrying out the strike. Investigators said the failure to refresh the targeting information and verify that the building was a legitimate military target went beyond mere carelessness.According to the report, the US would have struck the school while knowing there was a real chance of hitting a civilian site, and would have behaved recklessly about the possibility that this would occur.In June, US President Donald Trump stated that "nobody" purposefully attacked a girls' school in Iran in February, pointing to an ongoing inquiry into the episode. Reuters had earlier reported that a preliminary internal US military inquiry indicated American forces were probably to blame for the deadly Minab strike in southern Iran.The Pentagon has since escalated the level of the inquiry but has not released any interim conclusions.UN investigators said the school was plainly a civilian site and found nothing to suggest it had any military use.The mission reached a comparable finding regarding a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd, which it said damaged nearby homes and a school and killed or wounded 22 civilians. It judged this strike, too, to have been indiscriminate and therefore a war crime.US central command said in a March statement that American forces carried out no strikes on Lamerd that day.Iranian crackdownThe UN mission's inquiry also concluded that Iranian authorities led a widespread and systematic campaign against civilians during the anti-government protests, including unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, and heavy curbs on freedom of expression.According to the Reuters news agency, the mission said it was unable to confirm the death toll independently, but believes the true number of dead and injured is likely considerably higher than the official figures of 3,038 killed and 25,000 injured.The government's response to the protests, which included violence, killings, internet shutdowns, and the use of capital punishment, was a major escalation compared with how dissent had previously been suppressed.Tehran has attributed the unrest to "terrorists and rioters" supported by exiled dissidents and by foreign adversaries, namely the US and Israel.US officials have consistently maintained that their military operations comply with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has repeatedly denied claims of systematic human rights abuses.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Aztec document goes on display in Mexico after 186 years
articles.summary: France's national library is lending the manuscript recounting the history of the Aztecs to Mexico.
articles.body:
A centuries-old document telling the story of the Aztec civilisation and its fall after the arrival of the Spanish conquistadors in pictograms is going on display in Mexico for the first time in 186 years.

The manuscript, known as Codex Azcatitlán, has been held in France's Bibliothèque Nationale since 1898, but had already spent decades outside of Mexico before that.

It is thought to have been drawn in the 16th Century - a few years after the arrival of the conquistadors in what is now Mexico - and is widely considered one of the most valuable and insightful tellings of the history of the Aztecs.

France has lent Codex Azcatitlán to Mexico to mark 200 years of Franco-Mexican relations.

In return, Mexico has agreed to lend another priceless document, the Codex Boturini, to France for display there.

The pictograms in the Codex Boturini narrate the story of the migration of the Aztecs, also known as Mexica, from their ancestral homeland to the shores of Lake Texcoco, where they built Tenochtitlán.

The temporary exchange of the two codices was agreed by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and her French counterpart, Emmanuel Macron, during a visit by the latter to Mexico last year.

Mexico has long lobbied for the return of historical artefacts taken from the country in past centuries.

According to Mexico's ministry of foreign relations, last year more than 2,000 objects were successfully repatriated.

The Codex Azcatitlán will be exhibited at the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City from Thursday.

articles.title: Two Massachusetts brothers started a junk-removal business as teenagers with a $4,000 pickup truck; four years later, it made $3.04 million in 2025 and is targeting $5 million in 2026
articles.summary: US News: A bike ride to a local dump led Massachusetts brothers Kirk and Jacob McKinney to start a business that has grown into a multimillion-dollar junk-remo.
articles.body: A bike ride to a local dump led Massachusetts brothers Kirk and Jacob McKinney to start a business that has grown into a multimillion-dollar junk-removal company.Kirk was a teenager when he found a pair of working speakers at the dump and became interested in finding and reselling unwanted items, CNBC reported.The brothers launched Junk Teens in February 2021 in Norwood, Massachusetts. Kirk was 17 and Jacob was a high school freshman. The company generated $3.04 million in revenue in 2025.“I was hooked. I just kept going back to the dump and, eventually, my bedroom looked like a mini hoarder’s house,” Kirk said. He began selling items found at dumps and on Facebook Marketplace as a side business.His interest in discarded items soon connected with a local demand for junk removal. Kirk said he met people at the dump who were willing to pay local teenagers to remove unwanted items from their homes. He left his grocery store job and asked Jacob to join him. The brothers then bought a used 2006 Ford F-150 pickup truck for $4,000 of their own money.“We didn’t really know that we wanted to start this business,” Jacob said. They initially took on other jobs, including landscaping and moving work. Junk removal and reselling eventually became the part of their work they found most enjoyable and profitable.From one to five dump trucksCustomers also showed interest when they learnt that Junk Teens was repurposing items instead of simply removing them. The business grew from its early pickup-truck operation into a company with five dump trucks and two locations in eastern Massachusetts covering Boston and the Cape Cod area.The company completed more than 5,500 jobs in 2025, mostly residential and commercial junk-removal work. The brothers said they generally charge $300 to $600 per job, depending on its size and the service required.Junk Teens now has 10 full-time employees and about 10 to 15 part-time employees. The workers are high school students, college students or people taking gap years. The brothers plan to add two more dump trucks later in 2026.Kirk and Jacob are also studying entrepreneurship at Babson College while running the company. In 2025, each paid themselves salaries in the low-to-mid six figures. Some of that money went towards their college tuition, while their parents covered the rest.“The money is great, but that’s not what the whole point of this is,” Kirk said. “We want to build futures for our friends, and we want to do what we love and not have to work at a job that we hate.”Learning business from parentsThe brothers had some business experience at home because their parents run a local tree service company. Kirk said this gave them an early understanding of administration and bookkeeping.“One thing that we were very fortunate for is growing up in a family business background,” he said. “We grew up watching our parents do all of that stuff for their business, and we would ask them questions in the beginning,” Kirk added.The brothers also used YouTube to learn how to run the company. Kirk said they searched for “how to start a junk removal business” and learnt about setting up the legal structure and putting aside money for taxes.Junk Teens later began posting its own instructional videos, including content about negotiating prices and deciding whether items should be disposed of, flipped or donated. The company now has more than 400,000 combined followers on Instagram and TikTok.Running business while in schoolIn the early days, the brothers worked around their school schedules. They sometimes handled only one or two jobs a week after school or at weekends. As the company grew, they hired friends, gave up hobbies such as playing video games and changed their schedules.Jacob said they became “really crafty” with their time. During his senior year, he negotiated a block of midday free time with his guidance counsellor because local dumps operated during school hours.The brothers sometimes parked their dump truck in the school car park. Kirk said they would ask teachers for forgiveness when they were late for class.The company nearly cleared six figures in profit during its first year, Kirk said. The brothers then bought their first dump truck and kept it and their pickup in their parents’ driveway. They also stored electronics, appliances, furniture and bicycles under a tarp. “Our parents were not happy with that,” Kirk said. In March 2023, Junk Teens began renting warehouse space for $1,450 a month.From $1.2 million to a $5 million targetJunk Teens crossed $1.2 million in revenue in 2024, Jacob’s final year of high school. “Being a seven-figure business-owner in high school felt pretty crazy,” he said.The brothers now focus mainly on administration and strategy and have not gone “into the field” in nearly two years, Jacob said. In 2025, they used marketing software, promoted employees into leadership roles and opened their second location in the Cape Cod area.The brothers said these changes helped Junk Teens more than double its annual revenue and almost double its annual profit in 2025.Running the business while studying remains difficult. Kirk said he has considered dropping out of college three times to focus on Junk Teens full-time. He stayed, partly for his parents and partly because of what he has learnt at college.“College has taught me things that business never will,” he said, referring to social and communication skills. “And life isn’t all about making money and having a successful business.”Junk Teens plans to expand across the rest of Massachusetts before eventually moving into other parts of the East Coast. The company is targeting $5 million in annual revenue by the end of 2026.The brothers are also open to franchising the business, bringing in outside investors or selling it in the future, although none of those options is part of their immediate plans.“I have a really strong feeling that after college, things are going to take off more than they ever have,” Kirk said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Bridges open up woodland near Canterbury to Kent's roaming bison
articles.summary: The crossings have doubled the habitat available to Kent's free-roaming European bison herd.
articles.body:
Bridges have opened in woodland near Canterbury, doubling the area available to a herd of free-roaming European bison in Kent.

The two crossings, in West Blean and Thornden Woods, allow the animals to access an additional 50 hectares of habitat, increasing their roaming area to 100 hectares.

Kent Wildlife Trust said camera footage had captured the herd using the bridges for the first time as they began exploring areas of woodland that were previously inaccessible to them.

European bison were introduced to the woodland in 2022 as part of a project involving Kent Wildlife Trust and Wildwood Trust.

Bison are considered to be "ecosystem engineers" because their natural behaviour, such as browsing, grazing, felling trees and trampling vegetation, helps to create habitats for other plants and animals.

Heidi Aguirregoicoa, bison and conservation ranger at Kent Wildlife Trust, said: "It's been fascinating to watch the bison gain confidence with the bridges.

"At first, they were cautious and their first crossing happened under cover of darkness, but they quickly started using them more regularly."

Rangers were already seeing their impact on the woodland, she added.

"Fresh paths are appearing through dense vegetation, bark is being stripped from trees and their dung is enriching the soil and supporting insect life," she said.

Two further bison bridges are planned as part of the wider project.

Kent Wildlife Trust said these would eventually expand the habitat available to the herd to 200 hectares.

The bridges have been designed to allow visitors to cross above while the bison can pass beneath.

People can stand on the bridges and look through the viewing hides for the chance to see the bison, rangers said.

articles.title: Eleanor Donaldson to appeal trial of the facts verdict
articles.summary: The Northern Ireland Courts Service confirmed that an application for leave to appeal had been lodged to the Court of Appeal.
articles.body:
Eleanor Donaldson has applied to appeal the verdict from her trial of the facts, which found she had done the acts in relation to all five charges she faced.

Four of those charges were of aiding and abetting the offending committed by her husband Jeffrey Donaldson.

The former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader was convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

The Northern Ireland Courts Service confirmed on Thursday that an application for leave to appeal had been lodged to the Court of Appeal by Eleanor Donaldson's legal team.

She faced a trial of the facts after being found unfit for a conventional trial on mental health grounds.

It ran alongside her husband's trial at Newry Crown Court in May and June.

She cannot be given a prison sentence but could be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge.

The judge from her trial is due to decide on this in October.

Jeffrey Donaldson's solicitor has said he is also to appeal against his convictions .

articles.title: Can Democrat Peter Crosby flip Utah’s GOP-held 2nd District? Here’s what new poll shows
articles.summary: US News: Democratic candidate Peter Crosby has 30.7 per cent support against Republican incumbent Blake Moore’s 32.4 per cent in Utah’s newly redrawn 2nd Congr.
articles.body: Democratic candidate Peter Crosby has 30.7 per cent support against Republican incumbent Blake Moore’s 32.4 per cent in Utah’s newly redrawn 2nd Congressional District, according to an internal poll released by the Crosby campaign.The survey, conducted among 762 registered voters from September 8-10, puts Crosby 1.7 percentage points behind Moore ahead of the November 3 general election, with the gap falling within the poll’s plus or minus 3.5 percentage-point margin of error, according to the campaign.However, the poll was commissioned by the Crosby campaign and is not an independent survey. About 25.07 per cent of respondents were unsure about their choice, while 8.53 per cent selected none of the listed candidates and 3.28 per cent chose another candidate.Party-wise breakdownAmong Republican respondents, Moore led Crosby 45.7 per cent to 18 per cent, while 24 per cent were unsure. Among unaffiliated voters, Crosby received 39.4 per cent support compared with 16.5 per cent for Moore, with 30.3 per cent undecided.The campaign said affordability and government accountability were the top concerns among those surveyed. It said 74.4 per cent of respondents expressed concern about affordability-related issues, while 69.8 per cent cited corruption, insider trading and related accountability concerns.The survey comes as Utah voters have also expressed dissatisfaction with several statewide political leaders.A separate Deseret News/Hinckley Institute of Politics poll conducted by Morning Consult in August found Gov. Spencer Cox's approval at 41 per cent, while Congress had a net approval rating of minus 30 points.That statewide poll, however, should not be treated as a direct measure of the Utah CD2 race. It surveyed nearly 800 registered Utah voters statewide, rather than voters specifically in the newly drawn congressional district.The Crosby campaign also pointed to the Utah Debate Commission's independently commissioned polling, which had not been released when the campaign issued its September polling announcement. articles.title: Bishop Auckland baby garroted and hidden beneath floor - coroner
articles.summary: The boy was found beneath floorboards in a 1910 paper with twine around his neck, an inquest hears.
articles.body:
A baby found beneath floorboards and wrapped in a 1910 newspaper was probably garroted shortly after birth, a coroner has said.

The skeleton of the full-term boy was discovered during the renovation of a building on Bishop Auckland's Fore Bondgate in July 2024.

A piece of twine wrapped around his neck raised suspicions for detectives, County Durham and Darlington Coroner Crispin Oliver heard.

After concluding it was most likely a homicide, Oliver said it was a "very sad and singular case". The boy, named Baby Auckland by authorities, has been buried in Bishop Auckland Town Cemetery .

His date of death was listed as 29 July 2024, the day he was discovered.

The inquest in Crook heard the building's owner, Peter Moody, was pulling up floorboards in the second floor living room when he saw an object wrapped in old brown paper.

He picked it up believing it to be a ball, but then "took a look and thought this is a baby," he said in a statement.

He could see a skull, bones and "the little feet", Moody said, adding he also noticed a piece of "garden twine" wrapped around the baby's neck.

Durham Police immediately launched an investigation, the inquest heard.

Det Ch Insp Mel Sutherland said forensic anthropologist Dr Micol Zuppello worked for several days to "painstakingly extract the body", with all but the tip of a toe and some small eye socket bones recovered.

Zuppello concluded the child was a full-term baby of between 38 and 40 weeks development and had been placed face down.

Sutherland said his aim was to identify the baby, what happened to him and when he was placed under the floorboards.

"We had quite a lot to look at with not much to go on," he said.

Acid testing of the child's teeth, a technique developed by the universities of Durham and Bristol, coupled with DNA analysis concluded the child was most likely male, the inquest heard.

Radio carbon dating found the boy dated from any time between 1655 and the start of the nuclear era 300 years later, the coroner heard.

Forensic pathologist Dr Louise Mulcahy said due to the limited remains, it was impossible to test if the child had any natural diseases or if he had been poisoned.

The skeleton showed no signs of traumatic injury, she said, and the cause of death was deemed to be "unascertained".

It was also not possible to determine if the child had been alive or was stillborn, the inquest heard.

Mulcahy could not say if the 3ft (1m)-long piece of twine, which had been wrapped three times round the child's neck, knotted and then looped round again, would have been tied tightly or loosely.

Sutherland said investigations continued to try and determine when the baby was placed beneath the floorboards.

He said the building was built in about 1890 and the child was wrapped in an edition of The Umpire from Sunday 19 June 1910.

The detective said the "most likely scenario" was the baby came from about the date of the paper.

Investigators also looked to see if they could find living or deceased relatives through official DNA databases but none came up, the inquest heard.

Two sisters came forward to say they believed they might have been related to a servant working at the building at the time, but they were found not to be a DNA match to the boy, the inquest heard.

Sutherland said they also considered using genetic genealogy, databases of people who had voluntarily given DNA to trace relatives and family histories, but that was not usually allowed in the UK.

"It was assessed we wouldn't get to the identification of Baby Auckland even if we used that technique," Sutherland told the coroner, adding: "We would still be some generations off."

Officers also looked into getting a knot expert to examine the twine, but the nearest was in the Netherlands and the cost would be too expensive and the findings unlikely to be of much use, he said.

Sutherland told the coroner he was not aware of any religious practices or midwifery techniques from the time which would have involved the tying of string around a child's neck.

The detective said the twine was only around the boy's neck and appeared to have been deliberately placed there.

"I would ask why you would do that to a child who is already deceased?" he added.

Oliver said it was unusual in the 21st Century to find it so difficult to answer all the coroner's key questions, namely who the deceased was, when and where they died and how they came by their death.

"This a very sad and singular case," he said, adding the police had "left no stone unturned".

The coroner said the "critical piece of evidence" was the twine and it "seemed unlikely" it would have been tied to a baby who was either stillborn or died of natural cases.

He said the "most likely explanation" was a "person in a position to care for him while he was most vulnerable... took the decision to end his life by means of strangulation using twine as a garrote".

"This was a homicide," the coroner said, with the baby never officially recorded as existing and "disposed of by means of concealment".

He also said it most likely happened in or around 1910.

"Clearly this was a terrible thing that happened to a defenceless infant," Oliver said, but he added it was "heart-warming" to see how people had "stepped up to do the right thing" after he was found.
